questions.question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the dot products by the square root of d_k?
questions.answer: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. Then their dot product, q · k = ∑_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i, has mean 0 and variance d_k [4]. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by 1/√d_k [1][4].

questions.question: What percentage of WordPiece tokens does BERT mask during masked language model pre-training?
When BERT selects a token position for masking, how is it replaced?
questions.answer:
According to the context provided [3][5], when BERT selects a token position for masking, it replaces the word in one of three ways:
1. 80% of the time, it uses the [MASK] token.
2. 10% of the time, it replaces the word with a random token.
3. 10% of the time, it keeps the word unchanged.

This process ensures that BERT is forced to maintain a distributional contextual representation for every input token during training.

questions.question: What are the two RAG model formulations introduced in the paper, and how do they differ?
questions.answer:
The two RAG (Research Augmented Generation) model formulations introduced in the paper are RAG-Token and RAG-Sequence [4][5].

RAG-Token is described as a standard, autoregressive seq2seq generator with transition probability:
\[ p'_{\theta}(y_i|x,y^{1:i-1}) = \sum_{z \in \text{top-k}(p(\cdot|x))} p_{\eta}(z|x) p_{\theta}(y_i|x,z,y^{1:i-1}) \]
To decode, this model can be plugged into a standard beam decoder [4].

RAG-Sequence differs in that the likelihood \( p(y|x) \) does not break down into a conventional per-token likelihood. Therefore, it cannot be solved with a single beam search. Instead, for RAG-Sequence, beam search is run for each document \( z \), scoring each hypothesis using \( p_{\theta}(y_i|x,z,y^{1:i-1}) \). This yields a set of hypotheses \( Y \), some of which may not have appeared in the beams of all documents. To estimate the probability of an hypothesis \( y \), an additional forward pass is run for each document \( z \) for which \( y \) does not appear in the beam, multiplying the generator probability with \( p_{\eta}(z|x) \). The probabilities are then summed across beams to get the marginals. This decoding procedure is referred to as "Thorough Decoding" [4].

questions.question: Which retriever and which generator does RAG use?
questions.answer: RAG uses DPR as the retriever [2][3] and BART as the generator [3].

questions.question: How many parameters does the BART-large generator used in RAG have?
questions.answer: 406M trainable parameters [5]

questions.question: Which Wikipedia dump does RAG index, how is it chunked, and how many documents result?
questions.answer: RAG uses the December 2018 Wikipedia dump [3][4]. Each article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, resulting in a total of 21M documents [3].

questions.question: What library and approximation does RAG use to build its MIPS index?
questions.answer: [2] The retrieval component \( p_{\eta}(z|x) \) is based on DPR [26]. DPR follows a bi-encoder architecture, where calculating top-k(\( p_{\eta}(\cdot|x) \)), the list of k documents z with highest prior probability \( p_{\eta}(z|x) \), is a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem, which can be approximately solved in sub-linear time [23].

questions.question: During RAG training, which components are fine-tuned and which are held fixed?
questions.answer: During RAG training, the document encoder BERTd is not fine-tuned; it is kept fixed. Only the query encoder BERTq and the BART generator are fine-tuned [4].
